Frighted Jonah trembles, and summoning all his boldness to his face, only looks so much the more a coward. He will not confess himself suspected; but that itself is strong suspicion. So he makes the best of it; and when the sailors find him not to be the man that is advertised, they let him pass, and he descends into the cabin.

For the instant he almost turns to flee again. Then the Captain knows that Jonah is a fugitive; but at the same time resolves to help a flight that paves its rear with gold. But at that moment he is sprung upon by a panther billow leaping over the bulwarks. Wave after wave thus leaps into the ship, and finding no speedy vent runs roaring fore and aft, till the mariners come nigh to drowning while yet afloat. And ever, as the white moon shows her affrighted face from the steep gullies in the blackness overhead, aghast Jonah sees the rearing bowsprit pointing high upward, but soon beat downward again towards the tormented deep.

But again he leaned over towards the people, and bowing his head lowly, with an aspect of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spake these words:

“Shipmates, God has laid but one hand upon you; both his hands press upon me. I have read ye by what murky light may be mine the lesson that Jonah teaches to all sinners; and therefore to ye, and still more to me, for I am a greater sinner than ye. And now how gladly would I come down from this mast-head and sit on the hatches there where you sit, and listen as you listen, while some one of you reads me that other and more awful lesson which Jonah teaches to me, as a pilot of the living God. How being an anointed pilot-prophet, or speaker of true things, and bidden by the Lord to sound those unwelcome truths in the ears of a wicked Nineveh, Jonah, appalled at the hostility he should raise, fled from his mission, and sought to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Tarshish he never reached. As we have seen, God came upon him in the whale, and swallowed him down to living gulfs of doom, and with swift slantings tore him along ‘into the midst of the seas,’ where the eddying depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down, and ‘the weeds were wrapped about his head,’ and all the watery world of woe bowled over him. Yet even then beyond the reach of any plummet—‘out of the belly of hell’—when the whale grounded upon the ocean’s utmost bones, even then, God heard the engulphed, repenting prophet when he cried. Then God spake unto the fish; and from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea, the whale came breeching up towards the warm and pleasant sun, and all the delights of air and earth; and ‘vomited out Jonah upon the dry land;’ when the word of the Lord came a second time; and Jonah, bruised and beaten—his ears, like two sea-shells, still multitudinously murmuring of the ocean—Jonah did the Almighty’s bidding. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!

“This, shipmates, this is that other lesson; and woe to that pilot of the living God who slights it. Woe to him whom this world charms from Gospel duty! Woe to him who seeks to pour oil upon the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to appal! Woe to him whose good name is more to him than goodness! Woe to him who, in this world, courts not dishonor! Woe to him who would not be true, even though to be false were salvation! Yea, woe to him who, as the great Pilot Paul has it, while preaching to others is himself a castaway!”

He dropped and fell away from himself for a moment; then lifting his face to them again, showed a deep joy in his eyes, as he cried out with a heavenly enthusiasm,—“But oh! shipmates! on the starboard hand of every woe, there is a sure delight; and higher the top of that delight, than the bottom of the woe is deep. Is not the main-truck higher than the kelson is low? Delight is to him—a far, far upward, and inward delight—who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms yet support him, when the ship of this base treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him, who gives no quarter in the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin though he pluck it out from under the robes of Senators and Judges. Delight,—top-gallant delight is to him, who acknowledges no law or lord, but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him, whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and deliciousness will be his, who coming to lay him down, can say with his final breath—O Father!—chiefly known to me by Thy rod—mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Thine, more than to be this world’s, or mine own. Yet this is nothing: I leave eternity to Thee; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?”
He said no more, but slowly waving a benediction, covered his face with his hands, and so remained kneeling, till all the people had departed, and he was left alone in the place.

“Terrors upon terrors run shouting through his soul. In all his cringing attitudes, the God-fugitive is now too plainly known. The sailors mark him; more and more certain grow their suspicions of him, and at last, fully to test the truth, by referring the whole matter to high Heaven, they fall to casting lots, to see for whose cause this great tempest was upon them. The lot is Jonah’s; that discovered, then how furiously they mob him with their questions. ‘What is thine occupation? Whence comest thou? Thy country? What people? But mark now, my shipmates, the behavior of poor Jonah. The eager mariners but ask him who he is, and where from; whereas, they not only receive an answer to those questions, but likewise another answer to a question not put by them, but the unsolicited answer is forced from Jonah by the hard hand of God that is upon him.

“‘I am a Hebrew,’ he cries—and then—‘I fear the Lord the God of Heaven who hath made the sea and the dry land!’ Fear him, O Jonah? Aye, well mightest thou fear the Lord God _then!_ Straightway, he now goes on to make a full confession; whereupon the mariners became more and more appalled, but still are pitiful. For when Jonah, not yet supplicating God for mercy, since he but too well knew the darkness of his deserts,—when wretched Jonah cries out to them to take him and cast him forth into the sea, for he knew that for _his_ sake this great tempest was upon them; they mercifully turn from him, and seek by other means to save the ship. But all in vain; the indignant gale howls louder; then, with one hand raised invokingly to God, with the other they not unreluctantly lay hold of Jonah.

“And now behold Jonah taken up as an anchor and dropped into the sea; when instantly an oily calmness floats out from the east, and the sea is still, as Jonah carries down the gale with him, leaving smooth water behind. He goes down in the whirling heart of such a masterless commotion that he scarce heeds the moment when he drops seething into the yawning jaws awaiting him; and the whale shoots-to all his ivory teeth, like so many white bolts, upon his prison. Then Jonah prayed unto the Lord out of the fish’s belly. But observe his prayer, and learn a weighty lesson. For sinful as he is, Jonah does not weep and wail for direct deliverance. He feels that his dreadful punishment is just. He leaves all his deliverance to God, contenting himself with this, that spite of all his pains and pangs, he will still look towards His holy temple. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not clamorous for pardon, but grateful for punishment. And how pleasing to God was this conduct in Jonah, is shown in the eventual deliverance of him from the sea and the whale. Shipmates, I do not place Jonah before you to be copied for his sin but I do place him before you as a model for repentance. Sin not; but if you do, take heed to repent of it like Jonah.”

While he was speaking these words, the howling of the shrieking, slanting storm without seemed to add new power to the preacher, who, when describing Jonah’s sea-storm, seemed tossed by a storm himself. His deep chest heaved as with a ground-swell; his tossed arms seemed the warring elements at work; and the thunders that rolled away from off his swarthy brow, and the light leaping from his eye, made all his simple hearers look on him with a quick fear that was strange to them.

There now came a lull in his look, as he silently turned over the leaves of the Book once more; and, at last, standing motionless, with closed eyes, for the moment, seemed communing with God and himself.
But again he leaned over towards the people, and bowing his head lowly, with an aspect of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spake these words:

“Shipmates, God has laid but one hand upon you; both his hands press upon me. I have read ye by what murky light may be mine the lesson that Jonah teaches to all sinners; and therefore to ye, and still more to me, for I am a greater sinner than ye. And now how gladly would I come down from this mast-head and sit on the hatches there where you sit, and listen as you listen, while some one of you reads _me_ that other and more awful lesson which Jonah teaches to _me_, as a pilot of the living God. How being an anointed pilot-prophet, or speaker of true things, and bidden by the Lord to sound those unwelcome truths in the ears of a wicked Nineveh, Jonah, appalled at the hostility he should raise, fled from his mission, and sought to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Tarshish he never reached. As we have seen, God came upon him in the whale, and swallowed him down to living gulfs of doom, and with swift slantings tore him along ‘into the midst of the seas,’ where the eddying depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down, and ‘the weeds were wrapped about his head,’ and all the watery world of woe bowled over him. Yet even then beyond the reach of any plummet—‘out of the belly of hell’—when the whale grounded upon the ocean’s utmost bones, even then, God heard the engulphed, repenting prophet when he cried. Then God spake unto the fish; and from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea, the whale came breeching up towards the warm and pleasant sun, and all the delights of air and earth; and ‘vomited out Jonah upon the dry land;’ when the word of the Lord came a second time; and Jonah, bruised and beaten—his ears, like two sea-shells, still multitudinously murmuring of the ocean—Jonah did the Almighty’s bidding. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!

“This, shipmates, this is that other lesson; and woe to that pilot of the living God who slights it. Woe to him whom this world charms from Gospel duty! Woe to him who seeks to pour oil upon the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to appal! Woe to him whose good name is more to him than goodness! Woe to him who, in this world, courts not dishonor! Woe to him who would not be true, even though to be false were salvation! Yea, woe to him who, as the great Pilot Paul has it, while preaching to others is himself a castaway!”

He dropped and fell away from himself for a moment; then lifting his face to them again, showed a deep joy in his eyes, as he cried out with a heavenly enthusiasm,—“But oh! shipmates! on the starboard hand of every woe, there is a sure delight; and higher the top of that delight, than the bottom of the woe is deep. Is not the main-truck higher than the kelson is low? Delight is to him—a far, far upward, and inward delight—who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms yet support him, when the ship of this base treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him, who gives no quarter in the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin though he pluck it out from under the robes of Senators and Judges. Delight,—top-gallant delight is to him, who acknowledges no law or lord, but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him, whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and deliciousness will be his, who coming to lay him down, can say with his final breath—O Father!—chiefly known to me by Thy rod—mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Thine, more than to be this world’s, or mine own. Yet this is nothing: I leave eternity to Thee; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?”
He said no more, but slowly waving a benediction, covered his face with his hands, and so remained kneeling, till all the people had departed, and he was left alone in the place.

modern_en.title: Chapter 9 — The Sermon
paragraphs: Father Mapple rose, and in a mild voice of unassuming authority ordered the scattered people to close up. "Starboard gangway, there! Side away to port — port gangway to starboard! Midships! Midships!"
There was a low rumbling of heavy sea boots among the benches and an even slighter shuffling of women's shoes, and then all was quiet again, every eye on the preacher.

He paused a moment, then kneeled in the bow of the pulpit, folded his large brown hands across his chest, raised his closed eyes, and offered a prayer so deeply reverent that he seemed to be kneeling and praying at the bottom of the sea.

When he finished, in prolonged, solemn tones — like the continuous tolling of a bell on a ship foundering at sea in fog — he began reading the following hymn. But as he reached the final stanzas, his manner changed, and he burst forth with pealing joy and exultation:
"The ribs and terrors in the whale / Arched over me a dismal gloom, / While all God's sunlit waves rolled by, / And lifted me deepening down to doom.
"I saw the opening jaws of hell, / With endless pains and sorrows there; / Which none but those who feel can tell — / Oh, I was plunging to despair.
"In black distress, I called my God, / When I could hardly think him mine; / He bent his ear to my complaints — / No more the whale did me confine.
"Swiftly he flew to my relief, / As though on a shining dolphin borne; / Fearsome, yet bright, as lightning shone / The face of my Deliverer God.
"My song forever shall record / That terrible, that joyful hour; / I give the glory to my God, / His all the mercy and the power."

Nearly everyone joined in singing this hymn, which swelled high above the howling of the storm. A brief pause followed; the preacher slowly turned over the pages of the Bible, and at last, laying his hand flat on the proper page, said: "Beloved shipmates, clinch the last verse of the first chapter of Jonah — 'And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.'"

"Shipmates, this book, containing only four chapters — four yarns — is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of the Scriptures. Yet what depths of the soul Jonah's deep sea-line sounds! What a pregnant lesson this prophet is to us! What a noble thing is that canticle in the fish's belly! How billow-like and boisterously grand! We feel the floods surging over us; we sound with him to the kelpy bottom of the waters; seaweed and all the slime of the sea is around us! But what is this lesson that the book of Jonah teaches? Shipmates, it is a two-stranded lesson: a lesson to us all as sinful men, and a lesson to me as a pilot of the living God. As sinful men, it is a lesson to us all, because it is a story of the sin, the hard-heartedness, the suddenly awakened fears, the swift punishment, the repentance, the prayers, and finally the deliverance and joy of Jonah. As with all sinners among men, the sin of this son of Amittai lay in his willful disobedience of the command of God — never mind now what that command was, or how it was conveyed — which he found a hard command. But all the things that God would have us do are hard for us to do — remember that — and so he more often commands us than tries to persuade us. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying of ourselves that the hardness of obeying God consists.

"With this sin of disobedience in him, Jonah flouts God still further by trying to flee from Him. He thinks that a ship made by men will carry him into countries where God does not reign, but only the Captains of this earth. He skulks about the wharves of Joppa, and looks for a ship that's bound for Tarshish. Perhaps there lurks a meaning here that no one has noticed until now. By all accounts Tarshish could have been no other city than the modern Cadiz. That's the opinion of learned men. And where is Cadiz, shipmates? Cadiz is in Spain; as far by water from Joppa as Jonah could possibly have sailed in those ancient days, when the Atlantic was an almost unknown sea. Because Joppa, the modern Jaffa, shipmates, is on the most easterly coast of the Mediterranean, the Syrian coast; and Tarshish, or Cadiz, is more than two thousand miles to the west of that, just outside the Straits of Gibraltar. Don't you see, then, shipmates, that Jonah sought to flee the whole width of the world from God? Miserable man! Oh! Most contemptible and worthy of all scorn; with slouched hat and guilty eye, skulking from his God; prowling among the shipping like a vile burglar hurrying to cross the seas. His look is so disordered and self-condemning that if there had been policemen in those days, Jonah would have been arrested on the mere suspicion of something wrong before he touched a deck. How plainly he's a fugitive! No baggage, not a hat-box, valise, or carpetbag — no friends come with him to the wharf to say goodbye. At last, after much dodging search, he finds the Tarshish ship taking on the last items of her cargo; and as he steps on board to see its Captain in the cabin, all the sailors stop hoisting in the goods for the moment, to take note of the stranger's evil eye. Jonah sees this; but in vain he tries to look all ease and confidence; in vain he attempts his wretched smile. The sailors' strong intuitions about the man assure them he can be no innocent. In their playful but still serious way, one whispers to another — 'Jack, he's robbed a widow'; or, 'Joe, do you see him? He's a bigamist'; or, 'Harry lad, I guess he's the adulterer that broke jail in old Gomorrah, or maybe one of the missing murderers from Sodom.' Another runs to read the notice that's stuck up against the post on the wharf where the ship is moored, offering five hundred gold coins for the capture of a parricide, and giving a description of his person. He reads, and looks from Jonah to the notice; while all his sympathetic shipmates now crowd around Jonah, ready to lay their hands on him. Frightened Jonah trembles, and summoning all his boldness into his face, only looks all the more a coward. He will not admit that he is suspected; but that in itself is strong grounds for suspicion. So he makes the best of it; and when the sailors find that he is not the man in the notice, they let him pass, and he goes down into the cabin.

"'Who's there?' cries the Captain at his busy desk, hurriedly making out his papers for the Customs — 'Who's there?' Oh! How that harmless question mangles Jonah! For an instant he almost turns to flee again. But he rallies. 'I want a passage in this ship to Tarshish; how soon do you sail, sir?' So far the busy Captain had not looked up at Jonah, though the man now stands in front of him; but no sooner does he hear that hollow voice than he darts a searching glance at him. 'We sail with the next tide,' he answered at last, slowly, still eyeing him intently. 'No sooner, sir?' — 'Soon enough for any honest man who goes as a passenger.' Ha! Jonah, that's another stab. But he swiftly calls the Captain away from that scent. 'I'll sail with you,' he says — 'the passage money, how much is that? I'll pay now.' For it is particularly written, shipmates, as if it were a thing not to be overlooked in this history, 'that he paid the fare thereof' before the ship sailed. And taken with the context, this is full of meaning.

"Now Jonah's Captain, shipmates, was one whose discernment detects crime in anyone, but whose greed exposes it only in the penniless. In this world, shipmates, sin that pays its way can travel freely, and without a passport; whereas Virtue, if a pauper, is stopped at every frontier. So Jonah's Captain gets ready to test the length of Jonah's purse before he judges him openly. He charges him three times the usual sum; and Jonah agrees to it. Then the Captain knows that Jonah is a fugitive; but at the same time he resolves to help a flight that paves its trail with gold. Yet when Jonah actually takes out his purse, prudent suspicions still trouble the Captain. He rings every coin to find a counterfeit. 'Not a forger, anyway,' he mutters; and Jonah is entered for his passage. 'Show me my stateroom, sir,' says Jonah now; 'I'm travel-weary; I need sleep.' 'You look it,' says the Captain; 'there's your room.' Jonah goes in, and would lock the door, but the lock has no key. Hearing him foolishly fumbling there, the Captain laughs quietly to himself, and mutters something about how the doors of convicts' cells are never allowed to be locked from inside. All dressed and dusty as he is, Jonah throws himself into his berth, and finds the little stateroom's ceiling almost resting on his forehead. The air is close, and Jonah gasps. Then, in that cramped hole, sunk too beneath the ship's waterline, Jonah feels a foreboding, like a herald, of that stifling hour when the whale will hold him in the smallest of the prison wards of his bowels.

"Screwed at its axis against the side, a swinging lamp gently oscillates in Jonah's room; and as the ship heels over toward the wharf with the weight of the last bales taken on, the lamp, flame and all, though slightly moving, still keeps a permanent slant in relation to the room; though in truth, being itself unfailingly straight, it only makes obvious the false, lying levels among which it hangs. The lamp alarms and frightens Jonah; as he lies in his berth his tormented eyes roll around the place, and this so far successful fugitive finds no refuge for his restless glance. But that contradiction in the lamp appalls him more and more. The floor, the ceiling, and the side are all awry. 'Oh! So my conscience hangs in me!' he groans. 'Straight upward it burns; but the chambers of my soul are all in crookedness!'

"Like one who after a night of drunken revelry hurries to his bed, still reeling, but with his conscience still pricking him, just as the plunging of the Roman racehorse only strikes the steel tags hung on it all the deeper into its flesh; like one who in that miserable plight still turns and turns in giddy anguish, praying God for annihilation until the fit has passed; and at last, amid the whirl of woe he feels, a deep stupor steals over him, as over a man who bleeds to death, for conscience is the wound, and there is nothing to stanch it; so, after sore wrestlings in his berth, Jonah's prodigy of ponderous misery drags him drowning down to sleep.

"And now the time of the tide has come; the ship casts off her cables; and from the deserted wharf the uncheered ship for Tarshish, heeling far over, glides out to sea. That ship, my friends, was the first smuggler on record! The contraband was Jonah. But the sea rebels; it will not bear the wicked burden. A dreadful storm comes on; the ship is about to break up. But now, when the boatswain calls all hands to lighten her; when boxes, bales, and jars are clattering overboard; when the wind is shrieking, and the men are yelling, and every plank thunders with trampling feet right over Jonah's head; in all this raging tumult, Jonah sleeps his hideous sleep. He sees no black sky and raging sea, does not feel the reeling timbers, and little does he hear or heed the distant rush of the mighty whale, which even now, with open mouth, is cleaving the seas after him. Yes, shipmates, Jonah had gone down into the sides of the ship — a berth in the cabin, as I take it — and was fast asleep. But the frightened master comes to him, and shrieks in his dead ear, 'What do you mean, O sleeper? Arise!' Startled from his lethargy by that dreadful cry, Jonah staggers to his feet, and stumbling up to the deck, grasps a shroud, one of the ropes bracing the mast, to look out at the sea. But at that moment a panther of a billow leaps over the bulwarks and springs on him. Wave after wave leaps into the ship like this, and finding no quick way out, runs roaring fore and aft, until the sailors come close to drowning while still afloat. And every time the white moon shows her frightened face from the steep gullies in the blackness overhead, aghast Jonah sees the rearing bowsprit pointing high upward, but soon beaten downward again toward the tormented deep.

"Terrors upon terrors run shouting through his soul. In all his cringing postures, the God-fugitive is now too plainly recognized. The sailors take note of him; their suspicions of him grow more and more certain, and at last, to test the truth fully by referring the whole matter to high Heaven, they fall to casting lots, to see on whose account this great tempest has come upon them. The lot is Jonah's; and once that is discovered, how furiously they mob him with their questions. 'What is your occupation? Where do you come from? Your country? What people?' But note now, my shipmates, the behavior of poor Jonah. The eager sailors only ask him who he is, and where he is from; yet they receive not only an answer to those questions, but also an answer to a question they did not put; and that unasked answer is forced from Jonah by the hard hand of God that is upon him.

"'I am a Hebrew,' he cries — and then — 'I fear the Lord, the God of Heaven, who has made the sea and the dry land!' Fear Him, O Jonah? Yes, well might you fear the Lord God then! Right away he goes on to make a full confession; at which the sailors become more and more appalled, but still they pity him. For when Jonah, not yet begging God for mercy, since he knew all too well the darkness of what he deserved — when wretched Jonah cries out to them to take him and throw him into the sea, for he knew that it was for his sake this great tempest was upon them, they mercifully turn from him, and look for other ways to save the ship. But all in vain; the indignant gale howls louder; then, with one hand raised to God in prayer, with the other they, not without reluctance, lay hold of Jonah.

"And now see Jonah lifted up like an anchor and dropped into the sea; and at once an oily calm drifts in from the east, and the sea goes still, as Jonah takes the gale down with him and leaves smooth water behind. He sinks into the whirling heart of such a masterless turmoil that he barely notices the moment he drops, seething, into the gaping jaws that wait for him; and the whale slams all his ivory teeth shut on his prison, like so many white bolts. Then Jonah prayed to the Lord from the belly of the fish. But look at his prayer, and learn a weighty lesson. For sinful as he is, Jonah doesn't weep and wail to be rescued outright. He feels that his terrible punishment is just. He leaves his rescue entirely to God, and is content with this: that despite all his pains and pangs, he will still look toward His holy temple. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not loudly demanding pardon, but grateful for punishment. And how much this conduct of Jonah's pleased God is shown when He finally delivers him from the sea and the whale. Shipmates, I don't set Jonah before you to be imitated in his sin; but I do set him before you as a model of repentance. Don't sin; but if you do, make sure you repent of it the way Jonah did."

While he spoke these words, the howling of the shrieking, slanting storm outside seemed to add new power to the preacher. Describing Jonah's storm, he seemed tossed by a storm himself. His deep chest heaved like a ground swell; his tossed arms seemed the warring elements at work; and the thunder rolling from his dark brow and the light leaping from his eyes made every simple listener watch him with a strange, quick fear.
Then a lull came over his expression as he silently turned the pages of the Book once more. At last, standing motionless with closed eyes, he seemed for a moment to be communing with God and himself.
But again he leaned toward the congregation, and bowing his head low, with an expression of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spoke these words:

"Shipmates, God has laid just one hand on you; both his hands press down on me. By whatever murky light I have, I have read you the lesson that Jonah teaches all sinners; and so to you, and still more to me, because I am a greater sinner than you. And now how gladly I would come down from this masthead and sit on the hatches there where you are sitting, and listen as you listen, while one of you read me that other and more awful lesson — the one Jonah teaches me, as a pilot of the living God. How Jonah — an anointed pilot-prophet, or speaker of true things, commanded by the Lord to sound those unwelcome truths in the ears of wicked Nineveh — appalled at the hostility he would stir up, fled from his mission, and tried to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Jonah never reached Tarshish. As we have seen, God came down on him in the whale and swallowed him into living gulfs of doom, and with swift, slanting plunges dragged him 'into the midst of the seas,' where the swirling depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down, and 'the weeds were wrapped about his head,' and the whole watery world of woe rolled over him. Yet even then, beyond the reach of any plumb line — 'out of the belly of hell' — when the whale ran aground on the ocean's deepest bones, even then God heard the swallowed, repenting prophet when he cried out. Then God spoke to the fish; and up from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea the whale came breaching toward the warm and pleasant sun and all the delights of air and earth, and 'vomited out Jonah upon the dry land'; and the word of the Lord came a second time; and Jonah, bruised and beaten — his ears, like two seashells, still murmuring with the ocean's countless voices — Jonah did what the Almighty told him. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!

"This, shipmates, this is that other lesson; and woe to the pilot of the living God who takes it lightly. Woe to the man whom this world lures away from his Gospel duty! Woe to the man who tries to pour oil on the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to the man who tries to please rather than to appall! Woe to the man whose good name matters more to him than goodness! Woe to the man who, in this world, does not court dishonor! Woe to the man who would not be true, even if being false meant salvation! Yes, woe to the man who, as the great Pilot Paul says, preaches to others and is himself a castaway!"

He dropped and fell away from himself for a moment; then, lifting his face to them again, he showed a deep joy in his eyes, as he cried out with a heavenly enthusiasm: "But oh! Shipmates! On the starboard hand of every woe there is a sure delight; and the top of that delight is higher than the bottom of the woe is deep. Is not the main-truck at the masthead higher than the kelson is low? Delight is to him — a far, far upward and inward delight — who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth always stands forth as his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms still hold him up when the ship of this base, treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him who gives no quarter in the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin, though he pluck it out from under the robes of Senators and Judges. Delight — top-gallant delight is to him who acknowledges no law or lord but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and deliciousness will be his who, coming to lay himself down, can say with his final breath — O Father! — known to me chiefly by Your rod — mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Yours, more than to be this world's, or my own. Yet this is nothing: I leave eternity to You; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?"
He said no more. Slowly waving a benediction, he covered his face with his hands and remained kneeling until every person had left and he was alone in the place.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 9 — Prædikenen
paragraphs: Father Mapple rejste sig, og med en mild stemme og en uprætentiøs autoritet bad han de spredte mennesker om at rykke sammen. »Styrbords gang, dér! Gå til side mod bagbord — bagbords gang over mod styrbord! Midtskibs! Midtskibs!«
Der lød en lav rumlen af tunge søstøvler mellem bænkene og et endnu svagere skrab fra kvindesko, og så var alt stille igen, hvert øje rettet mod prædikanten.

Han holdt en kort pause, knælede så i prædikestolens bov, lagde sine store brune hænder over kors på brystet, løftede sine lukkede øjne og bad en bøn så dybt ærbødig, at han syntes at knæle og bede på havets bund.

Da han var færdig, begyndte han med langsomme, højtidelige toner — som den uafbrudte klemten fra en klokke på et skib, der er ved at synke i tågen på havet — at læse følgende salme. Men da han nåede de sidste vers, ændrede hans måde sig, og han brød ud i klingende glæde og jubel:
»Hvalens ribben og rædsler / hvælvede sig over mig i et dystert mørke, / mens alle Guds solbelyste bølger rullede forbi / og løftede mig dybere ned mod undergangen.
»Jeg så helvedes åbne gab, / med endeløse plager og sorger der; / ingen kan sige, hvordan det er, uden dem der har følt det — / ak, jeg styrtede mod fortvivlelsen.
»I sort nød kaldte jeg på min Gud, / dengang jeg knap nok kunne tænke på ham som min; / han bøjede øret mod mine klager — / og hvalen holdt mig ikke fanget mere.
»Hurtigt fløj han mig til hjælp, / som båret af en skinnende delfin; / frygtindgydende og dog strålende som lyn / lyste min Befrier Guds ansigt.
»Min sang skal for evigt fortælle / om den forfærdelige, den glædelige time; / jeg giver Gud æren, / hans er al barmhjertighed og al magt.«

Næsten alle sang med på denne salme, så den løftede sig højt over stormens hylen. Der blev en kort pause. Prædikanten bladrede langsomt i Bibelen, og til sidst lagde han hånden fladt på den rette side og sagde: »Kære skibskammerater, surr jer fast til sidste vers i Jonahs første kapitel — ›Og Gud havde beredt en stor fisk til at sluge Jonah.‹«

»Skibskammerater, denne bog på kun fire kapitler — fire fortællinger — er en af de mindste kordeler i Skriftens mægtige trosse. Men hvilke dybder af sjælen Jonahs lange lodline lodder! Hvilken rig lære er denne profet for os! Hvilken ædel ting er den lovsang i fiskens bug! Så bølgende og stormende storslået! Vi mærker flodens vande bruse over os; vi lodder med ham ned til vandets tangbevoksede bund; tang og al havets slim er rundt om os! Men hvad er det for en lære, Jonahs bog giver? Skibskammerater, den er tostrenget: en lære for os alle som syndige mennesker og en lære for mig som lods for den levende Gud. For os alle som syndige mennesker er den en lære, fordi den er historien om Jonahs synd, hans hårde hjerte, hans pludselig vakte frygt, hans hurtige straf, hans omvendelse, hans bønner og til sidst hans frelse og glæde. Som med alle syndere blandt mennesker bestod denne Amittais søns synd i hans egenrådige ulydighed mod Guds bud — lad os nu ikke spørge, hvad budet var, eller hvordan det blev givet — som han fandt hårdt. Men alt det, Gud vil have os til at gøre, er hårdt for os at gøre — husk det — og derfor befaler han os oftere, end han forsøger at overtale os. Og hvis vi adlyder Gud, må vi være ulydige mod os selv; og det er i denne ulydighed mod os selv, at det hårde ved at adlyde Gud består.

»Med denne ulydigheds synd i sig håner Jonah Gud endnu mere ved at prøve at flygte fra ham. Han tror, at et skib bygget af mennesker kan føre ham til lande, hvor Gud ikke hersker, men kun jordens kaptajner. Han lusker rundt på kajerne i Joppa og leder efter et skib, der skal til Tarshish. Måske gemmer der sig en mening her, som ingen har lagt mærke til før nu. Efter alt at dømme kan Tarshish ikke have været nogen anden by end det nuværende Cadiz. Det er de lærdes mening. Og hvor ligger Cadiz, skibskammerater? Cadiz ligger i Spanien; så langt væk fra Joppa ad søvejen, som Jonah overhovedet kunne have sejlet i de gamle dage, da Atlanterhavet næsten var et ukendt hav. For Joppa, det nuværende Jaffa, skibskammerater, ligger ved Middelhavets allerøstligste kyst, den syriske kyst; og Tarshish eller Cadiz ligger mere end to tusind engelske mil vest for den, lige uden for Gibraltarstrædet. Kan I så ikke se, skibskammerater, at Jonah prøvede at flygte hele verdens bredde væk fra Gud? Elendige menneske! Åh! Mest foragtelige og værd at spytte på; med hat trukket ned i panden og skyldigt blik, luskende væk fra sin Gud; strejfende rundt mellem skibene som en lav indbrudstyv i hast med at nå over havet. Hans udseende er så forvirret og selvdømmende, at hvis der havde været politibetjente i de dage, ville Jonah være blevet anholdt på blot mistanke om, at der var noget galt, før han nåede at sætte foden på et dæk. Hvor tydeligt han er en flygtning! Ingen bagage, ikke en hatteæske, kuffert eller rejsetaske — ingen venner følger med ham ned til kajen for at sige farvel. Til sidst, efter megen undvigende søgen, finder han skibet til Tarshish, mens det tager de sidste dele af sin last ombord; og da han går om bord for at træffe kaptajnen i kahytten, holder alle matroserne et øjeblik op med at hejse varerne ind for at tage den fremmedes onde blik i øjesyn. Jonah ser det; men forgæves prøver han at se helt rolig og tryg ud; forgæves forsøger han sit elendige smil. Matrosernes stærke fornemmelse for manden fortæller dem, at han umuligt kan være uskyldig. På deres muntre, men alligevel alvorlige måde hvisker den ene til den anden — ›Jack, han har røvet en enke‹; eller: ›Joe, kan du se ham? Han er bigamist‹; eller: ›Harry, min dreng, jeg tror, han er ægteskabsbryderen, der brød ud af fængslet i gamle Gomorrah, eller måske en af de forsvundne mordere fra Sodom.‹ En anden løber hen for at læse den bekendtgørelse, der er sat op på pælen på kajen, hvor skibet ligger fortøjet, og som tilbyder fem hundrede guldmønter for at fange en fadermorder og giver en beskrivelse af hans person. Han læser og ser fra Jonah til bekendtgørelsen, mens alle hans medfølende skibskammerater nu trænger sig om Jonah, klar til at lægge hånd på ham. Den forskrækkede Jonah skælver, og idet han samler alt sit mod i ansigtet, ser han bare endnu mere fej ud. Han vil ikke indrømme, at han er mistænkt; men det er i sig selv stærk grund til mistanke. Så han gør det bedste ud af det; og da matroserne finder ud af, at han ikke er manden fra bekendtgørelsen, lader de ham passere, og han går ned i kahytten.

»›Hvem er der?‹ råber kaptajnen ved sit travle skrivebord, hvor han i hast udfylder sine papirer til tolden — ›Hvem er der?‹ Åh! Hvor dette uskyldige spørgsmål piner Jonah! I et øjeblik vender han næsten om for at flygte igen. Men han tager sig sammen. ›Jeg vil have en plads på dette skib til Tarshish; hvornår sejler De, kaptajn?‹ Indtil nu havde den travle kaptajn ikke set op på Jonah, selv om manden nu står lige foran ham; men så snart han hører den hule stemme, sender han ham et gennemborende blik. ›Vi sejler med næste tidevand,‹ svarede han til sidst langsomt, mens han stadig stirrede intenst på ham. ›Ikke før, kaptajn?‹ — ›Tidligt nok for enhver ærlig mand, der rejser som passager.‹ Ha! Jonah, det er endnu et stik. Men han får hurtigt kaptajnen væk fra det spor. ›Jeg sejler med Dem,‹ siger han — ›overfarten, hvor meget koster den? Jeg betaler med det samme.‹ For det står netop skrevet, skibskammerater, som var det noget, man ikke måtte overse i denne beretning, ›at han betalte fragten derfor‹, før skibet sejlede. Og set i sammenhæng er dette fuldt af betydning.

»Nu var Jonahs kaptajn, skibskammerater, en mand, hvis skarpsindighed opdager forbrydelse hos enhver, men hvis grådighed kun afslører den hos de pengeløse. I denne verden, skibskammerater, kan synd, der betaler for sig, rejse frit og uden pas; hvorimod Dyden, hvis den er fattig, bliver standset ved enhver grænse. Så Jonahs kaptajn gør sig klar til at prøve længden af Jonahs pung, før han dømmer ham åbent. Han tager tre gange den sædvanlige sum; og Jonah går med til det. Så ved kaptajnen, at Jonah er en flygtning; men samtidig beslutter han at hjælpe en flugt, der brolægger sit spor med guld. Men da Jonah virkelig tager sin pung frem, plager forsigtige mistanker stadig kaptajnen. Han klinger hver mønt for at finde en falsk. ›I hvert fald ikke en falskmøntner,‹ mumler han; og Jonah bliver skrevet op til overfarten. ›Vis mig min kahyt, kaptajn,‹ siger Jonah nu; ›jeg er rejsetrættet; jeg må have søvn.‹ ›Det ser man,‹ siger kaptajnen; ›der er dit rum.‹ Jonah går ind og vil låse døren, men låsen har ingen nøgle. Da kaptajnen hører ham fumle tåbeligt dér, ler han stille for sig selv og mumler noget om, at dørene til fangers celler aldrig må kunne låses indefra. Klædt på og støvet som han er, kaster Jonah sig ned i sin køje og finder, at den lille kahyts loft næsten hviler på hans pande. Luften er lummer, og Jonah gisper. Og i det snævre hul, der desuden ligger under skibets vandlinje, føler Jonah en anelse, som en herold, om den kvælende time, hvor hvalen vil holde ham i det mindste af sit indvolds fangerum.

»Skruet fast i sin akse til siden svinger en hængelampe blidt i Jonahs rum; og mens skibet hælder over mod kajen under vægten af de sidste baller, der er taget ombord, holder lampen, flamme og det hele, selv om den bevæger sig en smule, alligevel en fast hældning i forhold til rummet; selv om den i sandhed, da den selv uvægerligt hænger lodret, kun gør de falske, løgnagtige vandrette linjer tydelige, som den hænger blandt. Lampen forskrækker og skræmmer Jonah; mens han ligger i sin køje, ruller hans plagede øjne rundt i rummet, og denne hidtil heldige flygtning finder ingen tilflugt for sit rastløse blik. Men den modsigelse i lampen forfærder ham mere og mere. Gulvet, loftet og siden er alle skæve. ›Åh! Sådan hænger min samvittighed i mig!‹ stønner han. ›Lige opad brænder den; men min sjæls kamre er alle i skævhed!‹

»Som en, der efter en nat med drukken svir skynder sig i seng, stadig svimmel, men med samvittigheden stadig stikkende, ligesom den romerske væddeløbshests spring kun slår de stålpigge, der er hængt på den, endnu dybere ind i dens kød; som en, der i den elendige tilstand stadig vender og drejer sig i svimmel kval og beder Gud om udslettelse, til anfaldet er gået over; og til sidst, midt i den hvirvel af jammer, han føler, sniger en dyb døsighed sig ind over ham, som over en mand, der forbløder, for samvittigheden er såret, og der er intet til at stoppe blødningen; sådan trækker Jonahs uhyre, tunge elendighed ham, efter hårde kampe i hans køje, druknende ned i søvn.

»Og nu er tidevandets time kommet; skibet kaster sine tove los; og fra den øde kaj glider det ujublede skib til Tarshish, krængende dybt over, ud på havet. Det skib, mine venner, var den første smugler, vi har optegnelser om! Smuglergodset var Jonah. Men havet gør oprør; det vil ikke bære den ugudelige byrde. En frygtelig storm bryder løs; skibet er ved at gå i stykker. Men nu, da bådsmanden kalder alle mand til at lette det; da kasser, baller og krukker rasler overbord; da vinden skriger, og mændene råber, og hver planke tordner af trampende fødder lige over Jonahs hoved; i hele dette rasende tumult sover Jonah sin hæslige søvn. Han ser ingen sort himmel og rasende hav, mærker ikke de svajende tømmer, og lidt hører eller bryder han sig om den fjerne susen fra den mægtige hval, som netop nu med åbent gab pløjer havet efter ham. Ja, skibskammerater, Jonah var gået ned i skibets sider — en køje i kahytten, som jeg forstår det — og sov tungt. Men den forskrækkede skibsfører kommer til ham og skriger i hans døde øre: ›Hvad mener du, o sovende? Stå op!‹ Skræmt op af sin sløvhed af dette frygtelige råb vakler Jonah på benene, og mens han snubler op på dækket, griber han fat i en vant, et af de tove, der afstiver masten, for at se ud over havet. Men i det øjeblik springer en panter af en bølge over rælingen og kaster sig over ham. Bølge efter bølge springer således ind i skibet, og da de ikke finder nogen hurtig vej ud, løber de brølende fra for til agter, til matroserne er lige ved at drukne, mens de stadig flyder. Og hver gang den hvide måne viser sit forskrækkede ansigt fra de stejle slugter i mørket oppe over dem, ser den forfærdede Jonah det stejlende bovspryd pege højt opad, men snart blive slået nedad igen mod det pinte dyb.

»Rædsler på rædsler løber råbende gennem hans sjæl. I alle hans krybende stillinger bliver Guds flygtning nu alt for tydeligt genkendt. Matroserne lægger mærke til ham; deres mistanke mod ham bliver mere og mere sikker, og til sidst, for fuldt ud at prøve sandheden ved at overlade hele sagen til den høje Himmel, går de i gang med at kaste lod for at se, hvis skyld det er, at denne store storm er kommet over dem. Loddet falder på Jonah; og da det er opdaget, hvor rasende de så bestormer ham med spørgsmål. ›Hvad er dit erhverv? Hvor kommer du fra? Dit land? Hvilket folk?‹ Men læg nu mærke til, mine skibskammerater, stakkels Jonahs opførsel. De ivrige matroser spørger ham kun, hvem han er, og hvor han kommer fra; men de får ikke blot svar på de spørgsmål, men også svar på et spørgsmål, de ikke stillede; og det ubedte svar bliver presset ud af Jonah af Guds hårde hånd, der ligger tungt på ham.

»›Jeg er hebræer,‹ råber han — og så — ›Jeg frygter Herren, Himlens Gud, som har skabt havet og det tørre land!‹ Frygte ham, o Jonah? Ja, du havde god grund til at frygte Herren Gud dengang! Straks fortsætter han med at aflægge en fuld tilståelse; hvorved matroserne bliver mere og mere forfærdede, men alligevel har de medlidenhed med ham. For da Jonah, der endnu ikke bad Gud om nåde, eftersom han alt for godt kendte mørket i det, han fortjente — da stakkels Jonah råber til dem, at de skal tage ham og kaste ham i havet, for han vidste, at det var for hans skyld, at denne store storm var over dem, vender de sig barmhjertigt fra ham og leder efter andre veje til at redde skibet. Men det er forgæves; den harmfulde vind hyler højere; så tager de, med den ene hånd løftet til Gud i bøn, med den anden, ikke uden modvilje, fat i Jonah.

»Og se nu Jonah blive løftet op som et anker og smidt i havet; og straks driver en olieglat ro ind fra øst, og havet bliver stille, for Jonah tager stormen med sig ned og efterlader blankt vand. Han synker ned i hjertet af et så herreløst oprør, at han næsten ikke lægger mærke til øjeblikket, hvor han — skummende — falder ned i de gabende kæber, der venter på ham; og hvalen smækker alle sine elfenbenstænder sammen om hans fangehul, som så mange hvide rigler. Så bad Jonah til Herren fra fiskens bug. Men se på hans bøn, og lær en tung lære. For syndig som han er, græder og jamrer Jonah ikke om at blive reddet med det samme. Han føler, at hans forfærdelige straf er retfærdig. Han overlader sin redning helt til Gud og er tilfreds med dette: at han trods al sin nød og smerte stadig vil se hen mod Hans hellige tempel. Og her, skibskammerater, har I sand og trofast anger; ikke højlydt at kræve benådning, men at være taknemmelig for straffen. Og hvor meget Jonahs opførsel glædede Gud, ses af, at Han til sidst frelser ham fra havet og hvalen. Skibskammerater, jeg stiller ikke Jonah frem for jer, for at I skal efterligne hans synd; men jeg stiller ham frem som et forbillede på anger. Synd ikke; men gør I det alligevel, så sørg for at angre det, som Jonah gjorde.«

Mens han sagde disse ord, syntes uvejrets hylende, skrå skrig udenfor at give prædikanten ny kraft. Da han beskrev Jonahs storm, var det, som om han selv blev kastet rundt af en storm. Hans dybe brystkasse hævede sig som en dønning; hans slyngende arme lignede de stridende elementer ved deres værk; og tordenen, der rullede fra hans mørke pande, og lyset, der sprang fra hans øjne, fik hver eneste enfoldige tilhører til at se på ham med en underlig, hurtig frygt.
Så lagde der sig en ro over hans ansigt, mens han tavst bladede i Bogen endnu en gang. Til sidst stod han ubevægelig med lukkede øjne og syntes et øjeblik at tale med Gud og sig selv.
Men igen bøjede han sig frem mod menigheden, og med hovedet dybt sænket og et udtryk af den dybeste, men mandigste ydmyghed sagde han disse ord:

»Skibskammerater, Gud har kun lagt én hånd på jer; begge hans hænder trykker ned på mig. Ved det dunkle lys, jeg har, har jeg læst jer den lære, som Jonah giver alle syndere; og den gælder jer, og endnu mere mig, for jeg er en større synder end I. Og hvor gerne ville jeg ikke nu komme ned fra denne mastetop og sætte mig på lugerne, hvor I sidder, og lytte, som I lytter, mens en af jer læste for mig den anden og mere forfærdelige lære — den, som Jonah giver mig, som lods for den levende Gud. Hvordan Jonah — en salvet lods-profet, eller taler af sande ting, som af Herren var befalet at lade de uvelkomne sandheder lyde for ørerne på det ugudelige Nineveh — skrækslagen over det fjendskab, han ville vække, flygtede fra sit hverv og forsøgte at undslippe sin pligt og sin Gud ved at gå om bord på et skib i Joppa. Men Gud er overalt; Jonah nåede aldrig til Tarshish. Som vi har set, kom Gud over ham i hvalen og slugte ham ned i levende afgrunde af undergang, og med hurtige, skrå dyk slæbte han ham ›ind i havets midte‹, hvor de hvirvlende dyb sugede ham ti tusind favne ned, og ›tangen snoede sig om hans hoved‹, og hele den vandige verden af jammer væltede hen over ham. Men selv dengang, uden for rækkevidde af ethvert lod — ›fra dødsrigets bug‹ — da hvalen lå grundstødt på havets dybeste knogler, selv dengang hørte Gud den opslugte, angrende profet, da han råbte. Så talte Gud til fisken; og op fra havets gysende kulde og mørke kom hvalen svævende op mod den varme og venlige sol og alle luftens og jordens glæder, og ›spyede Jonah ud på det tørre land‹; og Herrens ord kom for anden gang; og Jonah, forslået og mishandlet — med ører, der som to konkylier stadig mumlede af havets utallige stemmer — Jonah gjorde, hvad Den Almægtige havde sagt til ham. Og hvad var det, skibskammerater? At prædike Sandheden lige op i ansigtet på Løgnen! Det var det!

»Dette, skibskammerater, dette er den anden lære; og ve den lods for den levende Gud, der tager let på den. Ve den mand, som denne verden lokker bort fra hans pligt over for Evangeliet! Ve den mand, som forsøger at hælde olie på bølgerne, når Gud har brygget dem til en storm! Ve den mand, som forsøger at behage frem for at forfærde! Ve den mand, for hvem hans gode navn betyder mere end godhed! Ve den mand, som i denne verden ikke opsøger vanære! Ve den mand, som ikke ville være sand, selv om det at være falsk betød frelse! Ja, ve den mand, som, som den store lods Paulus siger, prædiker for andre og selv er en forkastet!«

Han sank sammen og faldt bort fra sig selv et øjeblik; så løftede han ansigtet mod dem igen, og en dyb glæde stod i hans øjne, mens han råbte med en himmelsk begejstring: »Men åh! Skibskammerater! På styrbord side af enhver ve er en sikker glæde; og toppen af den glæde er højere, end bunden af veen er dyb. Er stengetoppen i mastetoppen ikke højere, end kølsvinet ligger lavt? Glæde er hans — en langt, langt opadgående og indadgående glæde — som over for denne jords stolte guder og kommodorer altid står frem som sit eget ubønhørlige selv. Glæde er hans, hvis stærke arme stadig holder ham oppe, når denne lave, forræderiske verdens skib er sunket under ham. Glæde er hans, som ikke giver pardon i sandhedens sag og dræber, brænder og ødelægger al synd, selv om han må rive den ud fra under senatorers og dommeres kapper. Glæde — bramsejlsglæde — er hans, som ikke anerkender nogen lov eller herre andre end Herren sin Gud og kun er patriot for himlen. Glæde er hans, som alle bølgekammene på den stormende pøbels have aldrig kan ryste løs fra denne sikre Århundredernes Køl. Og evig glæde og sødme skal være hans, som, når han skal lægge sig til hvile, med sit sidste åndedrag kan sige — O Fader! — som jeg mest kender ved Din ris — dødelig eller udødelig, her dør jeg. Jeg har stræbt efter at være Din, mere end at være denne verdens eller min egen. Men dette er intet: jeg overlader evigheden til Dig; for hvad er et menneske, at det skulle leve sin Guds livstid ud?«
Han sagde ikke mere. Langsomt løftede han hånden til en velsignelse, skjulte ansigtet i hænderne og blev knælende, indtil hver eneste person var gået, og han var alene i rummet.
